title: Multi-Threading with POSIX pthreads & Thread Safety
summary: Master concurrent programming with POSIX pthreads: thread creation, joining, mutexes for mutual exclusion, race condition avoidance, and condition variables.
learningObjectives: Spawn and join concurrent POSIX threads with pthread_create and pthread_join
Protect shared state with pthread_mutex_t to eliminate data races
Coordinate worker threads using pthread_cond_t condition variables
prerequisiteConcepts: Completion of Lesson 5: File Descriptors & Error Handling

sections.heading: 1. Threads, Race Conditions and Mutex Synchronization
sections.content:
POSIX Threads (`pthread`) provide standardized multithreading in C. Unlike processes (which have isolated virtual address spaces), threads within the same process share the same text, data, and heap segments.

**The Race Condition Problem:**
When two threads increment a shared counter (`counter++`) simultaneously without synchronization, a data race occurs. At the machine level, `counter++` consists of three distinct CPU instructions:
1. Load variable from memory into CPU register.
2. Increment register value.
3. Store register value back to memory.

If a thread context switch happens between steps 1 and 3, one thread's update overwrites the other, causing silent data corruption!

**Mutexes (Mutual Exclusion):**
A `pthread_mutex_t` guarantees that only one thread can execute a critical section at any given time. Other threads attempting to lock the mutex will sleep until the owning thread unlocks it.

codeExamples.code:
RACE CONDITION vs MUTEX SYNCHRONIZATION:
WITHOUT MUTEX (Data Race):
Thread 1: [Read: 10] ---> [Add 1: 11] --------------> [Write: 11] (CORRUPTED)
Thread 2: -------> [Read: 10] ---> [Add 1: 11] -> [Write: 11]

WITH MUTEX (Serialized Execution):
Thread 1: [LOCK MUTEX] -> [Read: 10] -> [Add 1: 11] -> [Write: 11] -> [UNLOCK MUTEX]
Thread 2: (Waiting...) ----------------------------------------------> [LOCK] -> [Read: 11] -> [Write: 12] -> [UNLOCK]
codeExamples.explanation: Mutexes serialize access to shared memory, preventing concurrent interleaved read-modify-write operations.

keyPoints: All threads in a process share the same heap and global data segments.
Protect all shared mutable state with a mutex to prevent undefined race conditions.
Always compile multi-threaded C programs with -pthread flag (gcc -pthread main.c).
commonMistakes: Deadlock: two threads locking two mutexes in opposite order.
Forgetting to unlock a mutex before exiting a function early.

sections.heading: 2. Thread-Safe Concurrent Counter with POSIX Mutexes
sections.content: This complete program spawns 4 worker threads that concurrently increment a shared accumulator 100,000 times each, demonstrating zero race conditions.

codeExamples.explanation: Demonstrates pthread creation, mutex initialization, synchronized critical sections, thread joining, and mutex teardown.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
Starting 4 threads, each performing 100000 increments...
Final Counter Value: 400000 (Expected: 400000)
Thread safety verified: SUCCESS (0 Races)

keyPoints: pthread_join blocks until the specified thread completes, ensuring clean resource reclamation.
Destroy mutexes with pthread_mutex_destroy when they are no longer needed.
commonMistakes: Passing pointer to loop index variable &i into pthread_create (data race on argument).

sections.heading: 3. Systems Architecture Blueprint & Production Verification
sections.content:
Mastering Multi-Threading with POSIX pthreads & Thread Safety requires continuous empirical verification. In production environments, verify that every memory allocation is accounted for, buffer boundaries are strictly honored, and execution logs provide deterministic diagnostics.

Key Operational Checks:
1. Validate inputs and boundary constraints before executing core business logic.
2. Structure error handling so failed operations release all acquired resources before returning.
3. Establish automated unit and regression tests that exercise edge conditions and stress boundaries.
keyPoints: Reliability in systems engineering is achieved by treating failure modes as first-class architectural concerns.
Document and verify performance invariants with repeatable benchmarks.
commonMistakes: Failing to profile and test under simulated peak load conditions.

exercises.title: Implement a Multi-Threaded Parallel Array Sum
exercises.objective: Distribute an array summation across 2 threads and aggregate the final total.
exercises.description: Split an array into left and right halves, compute partial sums in parallel threads, and combine the results.
instructions: Define struct WorkerArgs with start pointer, count, and partial_sum result.
Spawn 2 pthreads, join both, and add the partial sums.
hints: Each thread writes to its own independent struct member, avoiding the need for a mutex during summation.
exercises.submissionRequirements: Complete all checklist items, test assumptions, and document verification rationale.
evaluationCriteria: Addresses the root architectural/technical challenge accurately
Follows defensive industry standards and edge-case validation
exercises.solutionExplanation: Independent thread outputs require no locks, maximizing parallel CPU cache utilization.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: What is the primary role of a pthread_mutex_t in multi-threaded C?

options.text: To guarantee mutual exclusion and prevent race conditions on shared memory
To allocate heap memory for new threads

knowledgeChecks.explanation: A mutex ensures only one thread executes a critical section at any time, eliminating data races.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: Which GCC compiler flag must be provided when compiling POSIX thread applications?
knowledgeChecks.explanation: The -pthread flag configures compiler preprocessor definitions and links libpthread required for POSIX threads.

recap: POSIX pthreads enable multi-core concurrent execution. Mutexes protect critical sections from data races, and pthread_join coordinates thread lifecycles.
